content: 1. The 2010 publication in Resource Health discusses global recommendations and guidelines for task shifting in healthcare systems, emphasizing its potential to optimize health worker roles and improve access to essential maternal and newborn health interventions. 2. A study by Walensky et al. (2011) compared counselor-based versus provider-based HIV screening in emergency departments, presenting findings from the USHER randomized controlled trial, which evaluated universal HIV screening in emergency room settings. 3. Champenois et al. (2012) described the ANRS-COM’TEST initiative, a community-based HIV testing intervention targeting men who have sex with men in non-medical settings, as published in BMJ Open. 4. Lorente et al. (2013) highlighted the ANRS-DRAG study, which expanded access to rapid, community-based HIV testing for men who have sex with men, emphasizing its urgency as a prevention strategy. 5. Fylkesnes et al. (2013) conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Zambia, demonstrating the strong effects of home-based voluntary HIV counseling and testing on acceptance and equity. 6. Molesworth et al. (2010) reported high accuracy rates for home-based community rapid HIV testing in rural Malawi, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 7. Bemelmans et al. (2010) described the implementation of universal access to antiretroviral therapy in Thyolo, Malawi, achieved through task shifting and decentralization of HIV/AIDS care. 8. Jackson et al. (2013) evaluated the quality of home-based rapid HIV testing conducted by community lay counselors in a rural district of South Africa, as published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society. 9. Iwu and Holzemer (2014) reviewed the clinical outcomes and self-efficacy of nurses involved in task-shifting HIV management from doctors to nurses in Africa, highlighting job satisfaction and effectiveness. 10. Leon et al. (2010) assessed the impact of provider-initiated (opt-out) HIV testing and counseling for patients with sexually transmitted infections in Cape Town, South Africa, through a controlled trial. 11. Kanal et al. (2005) evaluated the proficiency of trained non-laboratory health staff and laboratory technicians in performing rapid HIV antibody tests, demonstrating their effectiveness. 12. Lloyd et al. (2013) examined the safety and effectiveness of a nurse-led outreach program for assessing and treating chronic hepatitis C in custodial settings. 13. Hill et al. (2008) discussed the enhancement of hepatitis C treatment capacity through integrated, community-based care models in Canada. 14. A 2017 UNITAID report explored the availability of hepatitis C medicines and diagnostics in the context of HIV/HCV co-infection, providing a scoping analysis. 15. Pant Pai et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review comparing supervised and unsupervised self-testing for HIV in highand low-risk populations, published in PLoS Medicine. 16. Krause et al. (2013) reviewed the acceptability of HIV self-testing through a systematic literature analysis, as published in BMC Public Health. 17. Figueroa et al. (2015) examined attitudes and acceptability of HIV self-testing among key populations, as detailed in AIDS Behavior. 18. Choko et al. (2015) conducted a community-based prospective study in Blantyre, Malawi, evaluating the uptake, accuracy, safety, and linkage to care over two years of promoting annual HIV self-testing. 19. A framework for effective national responses to HIV/AIDS prevention, care, treatment, and support in prison settings was outlined in a 2017 publication. 20. A 2013 policy brief by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime provided a comprehensive package of interventions for HIV prevention, treatment, and care in prisons and other closed settings. 21. Grebely et al. (2015) discussed strategies to expand access to prevention, care, and treatment for hepatitis C among people who inject drugs, as published in the International Journal of Drug Policy. 22. WHO guidelines emphasized integrating collaborative TB and HIV services within a comprehensive care package for people who inject drugs, accessed in 2017. 23. Benhamou et al. (1999) investigated liver fibrosis progression in patients co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C, as part of the Multivirc Group study. 24. Di Martino et al. (2001) conducted a long-term retrospective cohort study on the influence of HIV co-infection on chronic hepatitis C in injection drug users. 25. Graham et al. (2001) performed a meta-analysis on the impact of HIV infection on the progression of hepatitis C, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 26. Lo Re et al. (2014) compared hepatic decompensation rates in antiretroviral-treated patients co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C versus those with hepatitis C mono-infection. 27. Ni et al. (2013) conducted a meta-analysis to determine whether increased hepatitis B vaccination doses improve immune responses in HIV-infected patients compared to standard doses. 28. Getahun et al. (2012) reviewed evidence for action on tuberculosis and HIV services for people who inject drugs, emphasizing harm reduction and prison-based interventions. 29. Getahun et al. (2013) discussed managing tuberculosis in individuals who use and inject illicit drugs, as published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 30. Padmapriyadarsini et al. (2006) examined the effects of anti-tuberculosis drugs on liver function in individuals co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B or C. 31. Liu et al. (2016) analyzed hepatitis B vaccination behavior and willingness among migrant workers from rural China, using protection motivation theory. 32. WHO provided guidance on couples' HIV testing and counseling, including antiretroviral therapy for serodiscordant couples, as part of a public health approach. 33. Patton and Tran (2014) reviewed the management of hepatitis B during pregnancy, as published in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 34. Celen et al. (2013) evaluated the efficacy and safety of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate during pregnancy for preventing vertical transmission of HBV infection. 35. WHO issued recommendations for HIV testing, counseling, and care for adolescents living with HIV, emphasizing a public health approach and considerations for policymakers.
